lessons.title: Barriers to Participation — and How to Remove Them

before.content_html:
Why Don’t People Participate?

Even when sport is on offer, many people never take part — or stop taking part. A barrier to participation is anything that gets in the way of someone being active. Understanding barriers is essential for sports clubs, leisure centres and national organisations because solving the wrong problem wastes resources. Identifying the right barrier for the right user group is the first step to removing it.

Key Fact

The nine barriers to participation are: employment and unemployment, family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of transport, lack of role models, lack of activity provision, lack of awareness, media coverage (gender and ethnicity), and personal factors such as low self-esteem or perceived risk.

Employment and Unemployment

People in full-time employment often struggle to find time for sport around working hours, especially shift workers whose patterns change week to week. Unemployed people face the opposite problem — time may be available but money is scarce. For both groups, sport that is free or very low-cost and offered at flexible times is most likely to work. A solution for full-time workers might be a leisure centre that opens at 6 am and offers 45-minute express sessions.

Family Commitments

Parenting young children, caring for elderly relatives, or running a household all compete with time for sport. Single parents and carers are particularly affected because they often have no one to share these responsibilities with. Solutions include ‘buggy fitness’ classes where children attend alongside parents, family membership schemes, and on-site crèche provision at leisure centres. Creche availability is frequently cited by mothers as the single most important factor in their ability to exercise.

Disposable income is the money left over after essential bills are paid. Sport has many hidden costs beyond a club membership fee: kit, footwear, travel, match fees, specialist coaching and competition entry all add up. For economically disadvantaged families, these costs can put participation out of reach entirely. Solutions include concessionary pricing (discounted entry for those on benefits or low incomes), kit-swap schemes run by local authorities, and Sport England ‘Active Communities’ grants that fund free holiday sport programmes.

Lack of Transport

Sport facilities are not evenly distributed across the country. In rural areas, there may be no swimming pool, athletics track or sports hall within reasonable distance, and public transport links may be poor or non-existent. Even in cities, night-time training sessions can end after the last bus. Solutions include minibus schemes organised by clubs, locating new facilities on existing public transport corridors, and encouraging car-sharing among club members.

Lack of Role Models

Seeing someone who looks like you succeeding in a sport increases belief that participation is possible. The absence of visible role models from ethnic minority backgrounds, disability sport, or specific genders at elite level can make sport feel ‘not for people like me.’ Solutions include targeted media campaigns, athlete ambassador programmes, and ensuring representative coaches at grassroots level. The visibility of British wheelchair tennis players and blind footballers at Paris 2024 inspired thousands of young disabled people to enquire about their local clubs.

Some user groups — such as carers, retired people or people with certain disabilities — simply find that no suitable programme exists near them. A leisure centre that offers only five-a-side football and high-intensity circuits has not provided for these groups at all. Solution: sports clubs can create targeted programmes (walking netball, sitting volleyball, adapted badminton) specifically for underrepresented groups.

Even where provision exists, people may not know about it. Lack of awareness is particularly common among newer immigrant communities who are unfamiliar with local sport structures, and among older adults who may not use social media. Solutions include targeted promotion through community centres, GP referral schemes, leafleting in non-English languages, and word-of-mouth outreach through trusted community leaders.

Media Coverage: Gender and Ethnicity

The sports that receive the most media coverage attract the most participants. Women’s sport and disability sport have historically received far less broadcast time and newspaper coverage than men’s sport. This creates a cycle: less coverage means fewer visible role models, which means fewer women and disabled people try those sports, which means fewer compelling stories for broadcasters to cover. The growth in women’s football audiences — the Women’s Super League regularly drew over one million TV viewers per match in 2024-25 — shows how media investment can shift participation patterns.

Key Fact

Examiners reward barrier–solution pairings. The question will say ‘identify one barrier for [user group] and suggest one solution.’ A barrier without a matched solution, or a solution without a linked barrier, typically scores only half the available marks.

Solutions: Facility Access and Adapted Provision

Physical adapted provision is essential for people with disabilities. This includes wheelchair-accessible changing rooms and pool hoists for swimmers, hearing loops at reception and in fitness studios, braille signage for visually impaired users, and coaching qualifications that cover disability sport. A sports facility that lacks a pool hoist has effectively excluded all wheelchair users from aquatic activity, regardless of how welcoming the staff are.

Solutions: Pricing, Promotion and Taster Sessions

Concessionary pricing reduces cost barriers: councils and leisure trusts typically offer discounts to people on Universal Credit, Job Seekers’ Allowance, or disability benefits. Taster sessions — free, no-kit-required introductory classes — lower the psychological barrier of trying something unfamiliar. Targeted promotion means advertising where the target group already is: leaflets at food banks for economically disadvantaged families, posters in GP waiting rooms for retired people, and social media campaigns in minority languages for ethnic minority communities.

A very common error is to list several barriers and then separately list several solutions, without showing which solution addresses which barrier. The question typically asks you to identify a barrier and then suggest how to overcome it for a specific user group. The mark is awarded for the linkage — barrier X causes problem Y for group Z; solution A removes barrier X by doing B. Always write your answer as a chain, not two separate lists.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are nine barriers: employment/unemployment, family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of transport, lack of role models, lack of activity provision, lack of awareness, and media coverage relating to gender and ethnicity.
  • Solutions must be matched to the specific barrier and user group — the linkage is what earns exam marks, not separate lists.
  • Adapted provision (hoists, hearing loops, braille signage), concessionary pricing, taster sessions and targeted promotion are the main solution categories to learn.

lessons.title: Popularity of Sport in the UK & Emerging Sports

before.content_html:
Why Are Some Sports More Popular Than Others?

Sport does not become popular by accident. The sports millions of people play and watch — football, tennis, athletics — are popular because a combination of factors has come together over many decades. Understanding these factors helps explain why some sports thrive while others struggle to find participants, and why new sports can suddenly break through. There are eight key factors that drive the popularity of sport in the UK.

Key Fact

The eight factors affecting the popularity of sport are: number of people participating, provision of facilities, environment and climate, live spectator opportunities, media coverage and range, high-level success of national teams or athletes, positive role models, and social acceptability.

Participation Numbers and Facilities

Sports with large numbers of participants generate income through club fees, kit sales and lottery funding — which in turn funds more facilities, coaching and development. It is a positive cycle: the more people play, the better the infrastructure becomes, which attracts even more players. Football has over 11 million registered adult participants in England, making it by far the most played team sport and explaining why there are far more grass pitches per square kilometre than tennis courts.

Provision of facilities is closely linked to participation. If there is no swimming pool within 10 miles, swimming participation will be low in that area regardless of other factors. The closure of public swimming pools in the 2010s led to measurable drops in adult swimming participation in those communities.

Environment and Climate

The UK’s mild, wet climate favours some sports and hinders others. Outdoor cricket requires dry summers; the British weather limits the playing season and discourages casual participation. Winter sports such as skiing need consistent snowfall — which is why the UK produces far fewer elite skiers than alpine nations. Conversely, the UK’s coastline and tidal rivers support a healthy sailing and rowing culture. Climate is not destiny, but it shapes which sports are practical to participate in without expensive facilities.

Being able to watch sport live — at a stadium, an athletics track, or a community pitch — creates emotional attachment and interest that drives participation. A child who attends a Premier League match is more likely to join a local football club than a child who has only watched from home. Premier League stadia regularly sell out at 50,000-plus capacity; the spectator culture this creates sustains grassroots interest.

Media coverage is perhaps the most powerful driver of popularity in the modern era. A sport broadcast on free-to-air television reaches tens of millions of viewers; one locked behind a subscription paywall reaches far fewer. The BBC’s coverage of Wimbledon annually peaks at around 9 million viewers and produces a documented spike in junior tennis sign-ups. The range of sports covered matters too: if a sport appears only once every four years (e.g. at the Olympics), it struggles to build sustained public awareness compared with a sport on television 38 weekends a year.

High-Level Success and Positive Role Models

When elite British athletes succeed on the world stage, participation tends to follow. Swimming participation in the UK rose noticeably after the 2012 Olympics — the “Ellie Simmonds effect” was cited by disability sport organisations as a factor in junior para-swimming club sign-ups. Similarly, Emma Raducanu’s 2021 US Open victory produced a 46% increase in tennis court bookings in the following months. Positive role models make sport feel aspirational and achievable, particularly for young people and for user groups who rarely see someone like them succeeding.

Key Fact

High-level sporting success creates what commentators call the ‘golden generation effect’ — a surge in grassroots participation after elite success. British Cycling’s dominance at the 2012 and 2016 Olympics correlated with a decade-long increase in recreational cycling across all age groups.

Social Acceptability

Social acceptability describes whether a sport is seen as normal, respectable and appropriate for different groups in a given culture. Historically, some sports were considered “not for women” (boxing, rugby) or “too aggressive for respectable families” (martial arts). Cultural shifts, growing media representation, and campaigns like the Rugby Football Union’s “She’s Got Game” initiative have changed these perceptions. Social media has accelerated this: when a sport looks fun and accessible online, social acceptability rises rapidly, particularly among teenagers.

Emerging Sports: What Are They?

An emerging sport is one that is new or rapidly growing in the UK and has not yet achieved mainstream status. Emerging sports typically have a small but enthusiastic participant base, limited facility provision, and are working to establish a national governing body. They often begin as recreational activities before formalising rules and competition structures. The pathway from emerging sport to established sport can take decades — or it can happen very quickly when social media amplifies the sport’s appeal.

Padel: Fast-Growing on UK Courts

Padel is a racket sport played in pairs on an enclosed glass-walled court about a third of the size of a tennis court. It originated in Mexico in the 1960s and became enormous in Spain and Latin America before spreading to the UK. Padel is easier to learn than tennis — the walls mean the ball stays in play longer, so beginners enjoy longer rallies — and it is intensely social. The UK had fewer than 100 padel courts in 2021; by 2025 that number had exceeded 1,000. Padel England secured recognition as the national governing body and affiliated to the Lawn Tennis Association for development support.

Pickleball combines elements of tennis, badminton and table tennis on a smaller court, played with a perforated plastic ball and solid paddles. It is particularly popular with retired people and older adults because the court is smaller, the pace is lower than tennis, and rallies are longer. In 2024, Sport England formally recognised Pickleball England as the sport’s national governing body — a key step in gaining access to lottery funding and local authority facility time. The number of registered pickleball players in England nearly doubled year-on-year between 2023 and 2025.

The factors driving pickleball’s emergence in the UK mirror those for any new sport: low initial cost (courts can be temporarily marked on any hard surface), easy-to-learn rules, high social enjoyment, and growing media coverage on YouTube and social platforms rather than traditional TV.

Not every new sport gains traction. Sports that require expensive specialist equipment, cannot be played in existing facilities, or have rules that are difficult to explain quickly often fail to grow beyond a niche. The absence of a governing body also limits growth — without official recognition, a sport cannot access lottery funding, government facility time, or schools programmes. Social media interest that does not convert to regular, in-person participation also fades quickly. The difference between an emerging sport and a short-lived trend often comes down to whether a committed volunteer community forms clubs, runs competitions, and lobbies for facility access.

The Olympic and Paralympic Movement

The Olympic and Paralympic Games are the largest peacetime gatherings on the planet — and behind the competition, medals and ceremonies lies a philosophy that has guided international sport for over a century. Understanding the Olympic movement means knowing its founding texts, its symbol and its values — because these are directly assessed and must be recalled precisely.

Pierre de Coubertin and the Olympic Creed

The modern Olympic Games were revived in 1896 by the French educationalist Baron Pierre de Coubertin. He believed that sport could foster international understanding and peace. The philosophy he articulated is preserved in the Olympic Creed:

Key Fact

“The most important thing in the Olympic Games is not to win but to take part, just as the most important thing in life is not the triumph but the struggle. The essential thing is not to have conquered but to have fought well.” — This creed is attributed to Bishop Ethelbert Talbot (1908) and was later adopted by Pierre de Coubertin as the guiding philosophy of the Games.

The Creed emphasises participation over victory, effort over outcome, and the character built through competition over the result itself. It is particularly relevant to athletes who finish outside the medal positions but who have competed to the best of their ability — a quality the Games celebrates through ceremonies such as the Best of the Games awards at Paris 2024.

The Olympic Symbol: Five Interlocking Rings

The Olympic symbol consists of five interlocking rings in blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white background. Designed by Pierre de Coubertin and first used in 1913, the rings represent the five continents of the world — Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania — whose athletes come together at the Games. The interlocking design expresses unity and the crossing of borders through sport.

A common misconception is that each ring represents a specific continent or that the ring colours match specific regions. In fact, the five colours (plus white) were chosen because every nation’s flag contains at least one of these six colours — the rings do not individually represent specific continents. The symbol is the most recognised sporting logo in the world and is a protected trademark of the International Olympic Committee.

The Olympic movement is built on three core values. The first is Excellence — the pursuit of being the best in body, mind and spirit; striving to perform at the highest level and to give of one’s best in whatever one undertakes. At Paris 2024, Dina Asher-Smith preparing for the 100m final — studying rivals, honing technique, choosing the right mental warm-up — embodied this value before she even reached the start line.

The second is Respect — respect for oneself, for other athletes, for the rules, for the environment and for the spectators. It is shown in post-race handshakes, in athletes challenging unfair calls through proper channels rather than confrontation, and in competitors carrying an injured rival across the finish line (as happened memorably at a 2019 World University Games race).

The third is Friendship — using sport to build bridges between people of different backgrounds, nationalities and beliefs. The Olympic Village at Paris 2024 housed over 14,500 athletes from 206 nations in one location, creating connections across borders that no diplomatic summit could replicate. Friendship is also seen in dual-nationality partnerships, mixed-relay events that pair athletes from different countries, and the tradition of trading national badges and pins.

Key Fact

Olympic values (three): Excellence, Respect, Friendship. Paralympic values (four): Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality. These are closed lists — they must be reproduced exactly. Students who mix them up or paraphrase them lose marks.

The Four Paralympic Values

The Paralympic movement has its own set of four values that reflect the distinctive experience of athletes with a disability competing at the highest level. The first is Courage — the bravery to compete, to push physical limits, and to confront any stigma around disability in public life. The second is Determination — the relentless effort needed to reach elite level, often against greater obstacles than non-disabled athletes face in access to coaching, funding and facilities.

The third is Inspiration — the power of Paralympic athletes to change attitudes toward disability in society, encouraging people with disabilities to participate and encouraging non-disabled people to reconsider assumptions about what the human body can do. At Paris 2024, British blind triathlete Dave Ellis and guide Luke Pollard’s gold medal was widely cited by UK disability charities as inspiring a wave of enquiries to para-triathlon clubs. The fourth is Equality — the belief that all people, regardless of disability, deserve equal opportunities to participate and compete in sport at every level.

Olympic and Paralympic values are not just abstract principles — they are embedded in specific campaigns and initiatives at local, regional and national level. At local level: a community sports club that runs a ‘have-a-go’ session for young people with disabilities is putting Equality and Inspiration into practice. At regional level: a county sports partnership that brings together athletes from rival clubs for a joint values day puts Friendship and Respect at the centre. At national level: UK Sport’s “Inspiring a Generation” legacy programme from 2012 continued to fund grassroots sport for a decade, directly linking Olympic success to community participation.

Schools can also embed these values through curriculum sport: competitive house events that reward Determination as much as results, or team challenges that deliberately mix year groups to build Friendship. The specification asks students to recognise examples at all three levels — so think local, regional and national when answering.

Students frequently swap the two sets of values. A common error is writing “Courage” as an Olympic value (it is Paralympic) or writing “Friendship” as a Paralympic value (it is Olympic). The simplest memory aid: Olympic values have three items (Excellence, Respect, Friendship); Paralympic values have four items (Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality). If you are asked for both sets in one question, list them separately with the correct heading.

What Is Etiquette in Sport?

Etiquette refers to the expected standards of behaviour in sport that go beyond the written rules. While rules tell players what they must do, etiquette tells them what they should do to show respect for the sport, opponents, officials and spectators. Etiquette varies between sports but always promotes fair and respectful participation.

Common examples of etiquette include shaking hands with opponents after a match, applauding good play by the opposition, walking off the pitch when injured without making a fuss, and accepting the referee’s decision without argument. In tennis, players wait for a break in play before retrieving an errant ball rather than disrupting a point. In cricket, a fielder tells the umpire honestly if they grounded a catch.

Key Fact

Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in sport. It includes acts like shaking hands after a game, applauding the opposition, and kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured — all gestures that show respect without being required by the rules.

Sportsmanship vs Gamesmanship

Sportsmanship means playing within the written rules AND the spirit of the sport. A player demonstrating sportsmanship competes hard but never at the expense of fairness or respect. Sporting behaviour includes playing to win within the rules, showing respect to the referee even when you disagree, and putting the welfare of an injured opponent above the advantage of the game.

Gamesmanship, by contrast, involves bending the spirit of the rules to gain a competitive edge — without breaking them outright. A football player taking a long time over a throw-in to waste a few seconds is using gamesmanship. So is a tennis player taking unusually long between serves to disrupt an opponent’s rhythm, or a cricketer deliberately moving in a fielder’s line of sight just before a delivery.

Many students confuse these two terms. Remember: sportsmanship is doing the right thing even when the rules do not force you to. Gamesmanship is doing something that is technically legal but goes against the spirit of the sport. A handy paired example to remember: kicking the ball out of play for an injured opponent (sportsmanship) versus slowing down a throw-in to waste time (gamesmanship). The question will often ask for “one applied example of each” — always give a specific sporting situation, not a vague description.

Values That Underpin Sporting Behaviour

Sporting behaviour is underpinned by shared values that sport is meant to promote. Fair play is the idea that competition should be decided by ability and effort, not by cheating. Respect means treating opponents, officials and teammates with dignity. Tolerance means accepting differences — in skill level, background or playing style — without hostility. These values explain why etiquette and sportsmanship matter beyond any single match: they preserve sport as a positive experience for everyone involved.

Key Fact

Sportsmanship requires playing within both the letter of the rules (what is written) and the spirit of the rules (what the sport is meant to stand for). Gamesmanship only respects the letter — it exploits gaps in the rules for personal gain.

Spectator Behaviour

Spectators play a major role in the atmosphere of any sporting event. Positive spectator behaviour includes cheering your team, applauding great play from either side, staying within designated areas, and following ground regulations. These behaviours create an enjoyable and safe environment for everyone — athletes, officials and fellow spectators.

Negative spectator behaviour, however, can have serious consequences. Hooliganism refers to disorderly or violent behaviour by fans. This can include fighting in and around stadiums, chanting abuse, throwing objects onto the pitch, or invading the playing surface. Hooliganism puts players, officials and other fans at risk. It can also lead to matches being abandoned, grounds being closed and the sport’s reputation being damaged.

Following the Hillsborough disaster in April 1989 — a crowd crush at Sheffield Wednesday’s ground that ultimately claimed 97 Liverpool supporters (95 died at the scene, a 96th in 1993, and a 97th in 2021; the campaign was historically known as Justice for the 96) — Lord Justice Taylor produced the Taylor Report (1990). Its central recommendation was that top-flight football grounds in England should become all-seater stadia, replacing terraces where standing spectators could become dangerously compressed. By 1994–95, all Premier League and First Division grounds had converted. All-seater stadia give every fan an assigned seat, reduce crowd surges, and allow stewards to monitor and remove individuals causing problems more easily. They are now considered an essential safety standard in modern football.

The shift to all-seater grounds also changed the culture of watching football. Individual ticketing reduced the anonymity that could mask troublemakers, and CCTV coverage became far easier to implement. Crowd segregation — separating home and away supporters — was formalised. Together, these measures contributed to a significant fall in football-related disorder from the 1990s onwards.

Spectators’ Responsibilities

Spectators are not passive bystanders. They have responsibilities to the performers, to officials, and to each other. Accepting referee decisions without confronting officials, avoiding language or actions that intimidate players, and not engaging in discriminatory chanting are all expectations placed on spectators. Ground regulations typically prohibit entering the field of play, and spectators can be ejected or banned for breaking these rules.

Some stadiums use “ultras” — highly organised and passionate fan groups, typically associated with European football. While many ultras create spectacular displays using flags, banners and coordinated chanting, the culture has at times been linked to disorder. The key distinction for the exam is between passionate support (acceptable) and threatening or violent behaviour (unacceptable and illegal).

Poor spectator behaviour has direct consequences: events can be cancelled or moved, clubs can be fined or have grounds closed, international reputations suffer, and broadcasters can lose confidence in covering the sport. On the other hand, a vocal and well-behaved crowd enhances the experience for everyone, creates a positive atmosphere and encourages participation. Examiners often ask students to explain how spectator behaviour can affect the sport as a whole — think about impact on the game, the club, the players and the wider image of sport.

before.content_html:
Why Do Athletes Use Performance-Enhancing Drugs?

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances that give athletes a competitive advantage. Reasons why athletes choose to use them include the enormous financial rewards available at the elite level, intense pressure from coaches, sponsors and national expectations, and the belief that “everyone else is doing it.” In some nations there has been state-sponsored doping — the Russian doping programme uncovered before the 2016 Rio Olympics is the clearest modern example. Injuries, quick recovery demands, and the desire to maintain performance as the body ages also push some athletes towards banned substances.

Key Fact

Reasons for using PEDs include financial rewards, competitive pressure, fear of falling behind rivals, and national expectation. Reasons against include health risks, ban from sport, reputational damage, acting as a negative role model, and the unfair advantage over clean competitors.

Why Athletes Should NOT Use PEDs

The case against PED use is equally strong. Many banned substances carry serious health risks: heart problems, hormonal imbalances, liver damage and psychological effects have all been documented. Beyond health, using PEDs violates the principle of fair play — clean athletes are denied a level playing field. Elite athletes are also role models: when they are caught doping, they send a damaging message to young people that cheating is an acceptable path to success. Athletes who test positive face heavy sanctions, public humiliation, and often have their results stripped retrospectively. The sport itself suffers reputational damage that can take decades to repair.

The Role of WADA

The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was founded in 1999 and is the international organisation responsible for the fight against doping in sport. WADA publishes the Prohibited List — updated annually — which names every banned substance and method. The list groups substances into ten categories (S0–S9): non-approved substances, anabolic agents, peptide hormones and growth factors, beta-2 agonists, hormone and metabolic modulators, diuretics and masking agents, stimulants, narcotics, cannabinoids, and glucocorticoids. Three further categories (M1–M3) cover prohibited methods (such as blood doping and gene doping). Beta-blockers and alcohol are listed separately as banned only in particular sports — archery and shooting for beta-blockers; archery and motorsport for alcohol. WADA sets the standards; national organisations — such as UKAD (UK Anti-Doping) — enforce those standards within their own country.

Key Fact

WADA was founded in 1999. It publishes the annual Prohibited List covering nine categories of banned substances and methods. In the UK, UKAD enforces the WADA Code on behalf of sport. The Whereabouts Rule is one of WADA’s most important enforcement tools.

The Whereabouts Rule

One of WADA’s most important anti-doping tools is the Whereabouts Rule. Athletes in the “Registered Testing Pool” must file quarterly Whereabouts submissions declaring where they will be — including a specific one-hour window each day (e.g. 7am–8am at home) when testers can arrive unannounced. Out-of-competition testing is considered vital because many PEDs are used during training rather than at competition itself.

If an athlete accumulates three missed tests or filing failures within any 12-month rolling period, this counts as an anti-doping rule violation — the same as actually failing a drug test. Athletes and their agents use the ADAMS (Anti-Doping Administration and Management System) online platform to submit Whereabouts information. The rule is demanding but is seen as essential to catch sophisticated doping programmes that use substances that clear the body quickly.

Students often know that athletes must “tell someone where they are” but cannot explain the specific mechanics that examiners want. Make sure you know three things: (1) it is a one-hour window per day where an athlete must be reachable; (2) athletes submit information quarterly in advance; and (3) three missed tests or filing failures in 12 months triggers a violation. The examiner report identifies this as the most commonly underscored knowledge gap on the doping topic.

Testing Methods

Anti-doping tests are conducted both in-competition (at events) and out-of-competition (during training). Athletes may be called for testing immediately after competing or visited at a training site without warning. Testing uses urine samples and blood samples. Blood passporting — tracking an athlete’s biological markers over time — allows authorities to detect patterns of doping even when a specific substance cannot be found in a single test. High-profile cases such as the Russian Athletics Investigation Federation (Russian athletes competed as “AIN” at Paris 2024 due to ongoing sanctions) demonstrate how systematic doping can be identified and punished at a national level.

Sanctions for Doping

Sanctions escalate depending on the substance involved, whether it was intentional, and whether the athlete has offended before. The typical sanctions ladder runs: formal warnings for minor first-time administrative breaches → fines → competition bans (ranging from one year to a lifetime ban) → criminal prosecution for those found trafficking banned substances. Results achieved during a doping period are typically annulled, meaning medals, records and prize money are returned.

High-profile cases illustrate the consequences: swimmer Sun Yang received an eight-year ban (later revised on appeal) for refusing to cooperate with anti-doping testers. Russia’s track and field athletes were barred from competing under the Russian flag at the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Olympics as a direct result of a state-sponsored doping programme. These cases reinforce that the consequences of doping extend beyond the individual to national sporting programmes.

Testing alone is not enough — education strategies are equally important. UKAD runs “100% Me” as an anti-doping education programme for young athletes, emphasising clean sport values and the risks of supplements. Schools and sports clubs are encouraged to discuss the ethics of doping openly. Role models who compete cleanly and speak out against doping are a powerful deterrent — young athletes are more likely to follow the example of athletes they admire than to respond to a rulebook alone. Nutrition education also helps athletes understand which legal supplements carry contamination risks that could produce a positive test.

lessons.title: Hosting a Major Sporting Event — Pre-Event & Bidding

before.content_html:
Types of Major Sporting Event

Not all major sporting events are alike. Before examining what it takes to host one, it is important to understand the three categories that appear on the specification. Getting these right is a common mark-scoring opportunity — and a common source of lost marks when students muddle the definitions.

Key Fact

The three types of major sporting event are: one-off (held in a host city once in a generation — e.g. the Olympic and Paralympic Games); regular (held repeatedly but in a different city each time — e.g. the UEFA Champions League Final); and regular and recurring (held repeatedly at the same venue — e.g. Wimbledon or the Monaco Grand Prix).

Students frequently swap the categories. Here is the clearest way to remember them: One-off — the same city is unlikely to host again in your lifetime (Paris previously hosted the summer Olympics in 1900 and 1924, returning in 2024 after a hundred-year gap from its last hosting). Regular — the event happens every year or two years, but in a different city: the Champions League Final has been held in Madrid, Istanbul, Paris and Wembley in recent seasons. Regular and recurring — same event, same location, every year: Wimbledon at the All England Club, the British Grand Prix at Silverstone. Always anchor each category to its named spec example in an exam answer.

The Nature of Participants and Spectators

Major events draw participants and spectators from very different backgrounds depending on their type. A one-off event like the Olympics attracts athletes from every nation on Earth and millions of global tourists — the 2024 Paris Games sold over 9 million tickets. A regular event like the Champions League Final has a smaller but intensely passionate fanbase that travels with the finalists. A regular and recurring event like Wimbledon draws a stable, often high-income, domestic and international audience to its permanent home in south London every June and July.

Why Host a Major Event? The Bidding Process

Cities and nations bid to host major events. For the Olympic Games, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) assesses bids from candidate cities. For the FIFA World Cup, FIFA makes the award to a national federation. Bidding requires submitting a detailed proposal covering: stadium and venue capacity, athlete village accommodation, transport links, security plans, broadcasting infrastructure, accommodation for spectators, and plans for what happens to facilities after the event — the legacy plan.

The bidding process is expensive in itself. Major bid campaigns can cost tens of millions of pounds before a single ticket is sold. Cities that lose their bid have spent that money for nothing, which is why many cities are now reluctant to enter the race. Several candidate cities withdrew from the 2024 Olympic bid before Paris and Los Angeles were selected for 2024 and 2028 respectively — concerns about cost and public opposition were the main reasons cited.

Key Fact

A successful Olympic or World Cup bid must address: venue and infrastructure; transport; security; accommodation; legacy planning; and financial viability. The IOC (for the Olympics) or FIFA (for the World Cup) evaluates bids against these criteria before awarding the event.

Pre-Event Positives

Even before the opening ceremony, hosting a major event delivers tangible benefits. Infrastructure development begins years in advance: new roads, rail lines, airports, and broadband networks are built or upgraded to meet event requirements. These improvements benefit local residents long after the event ends. Construction employment surges as stadiums, athlete villages, and media centres are built — providing thousands of jobs in an often short space of time.

Commercial investment flows into the host city as businesses respond to the opportunity of an arriving global audience. Hotels, restaurants and retail all benefit from advance bookings. The host nation also gains international profile and prestige — the Paris 2024 Games showcased France on the world stage, with the opening ceremony along the Seine attracting a global television audience estimated at 1.5 billion viewers. Tourism in the months and years following the event can also increase, as the host city gains new visibility.

Not everyone is delighted when their city wins a major event bid. Cost overruns are almost universal in Olympic host cities: the Paris 2024 organising committee budget reached around €4.48 billion, while total French state spending including infrastructure and security came to roughly €6.6 billion according to the French Court of Auditors’ 2025 report. Taxpayers bear most of this gap. Displacement is another concern: building venues and athlete villages often requires demolishing housing in less affluent areas, with residents relocated — sometimes with inadequate compensation. Local communities may face years of construction noise, disrupted roads and reduced access to their own neighbourhood. Political opposition can also mobilise: residents may vote or campaign against the event, causing friction between government ambitions and public sentiment.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a 'regular and recurring' major sporting event?
A) The FIFA World Cup
B) The UEFA Champions League Final
C) The Summer Olympic Games
D) Wimbledon
practice_questions.marks:
D) Wimbledon [1 mark]
(Wimbledon is held every year at the same venue — the All England Club. The World Cup and Champions League Final are 'regular' events held in different locations. The Olympics is a 'one-off' event.)

practice_questions.text: State two positive impacts for a host city in the period before a major sporting event takes place.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct positive (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
- Infrastructure development (new roads, rail, airports)
- Increased construction employment / job creation
- Commercial investment / business growth
- International profile / media attention raised pre-event
- Tourism bookings increase in advance of the event
- Urban regeneration of the host area
Do not award a second mark for the same point restated (e.g. 'jobs' and 'more workers employed' = 1 mark only).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a 'one-off' and a 'regular' major sporting event. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for correct definition of one-off (held in a host city once in a generation / same city very unlikely to host again for many decades). Award 1 mark for correct definition of regular (held repeatedly in different cities each time). Award 1 mark for a correct named example of each:
- One-off: Olympic / Paralympic Games, FIFA World Cup, Commonwealth Games
- Regular: UEFA Champions League Final, World Athletics Championships, Rugby World Cup
Do not award for 'Wimbledon' as a regular example — it is regular and recurring.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why a city government might have concerns about bidding for the right to host the Summer Olympics. Use examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit two distinct concerns with development:
- Cost overruns: Olympic budgets almost always exceed initial estimates — Paris 2024 grew from ~3.6bn to ~8.8bn euros. Taxpayers fund the gap.
- Displacement and community disruption: building venues requires relocating residents, often from lower-income areas, who may receive inadequate compensation.
- Political opposition: public may resist via protest or referendum, causing reputational and governance problems for the host government.
- Bid cost with no guarantee: a bid campaign alone costs tens of millions; a losing city gets nothing back.
A named example is required for the top marks. An answer without any named example is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Thornfield City Council is considering bidding for the right to host a major international athletics championship. Some councillors are in favour; others are opposed.

Discuss the pre-event advantages and disadvantages a host city like Thornfield would need to consider before submitting its bid.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion addressing at least two distinct pre-event advantages and two distinct disadvantages. Points are developed and interact with each other (e.g. infrastructure benefit has to be weighed against cost of building it). Applied context used. Points are not just listed but linked into a reasoned argument.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two valid points on each side with some development. Limited interaction between points. May not address all key areas.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid points identified but little development. One-sided or near-one-sided.

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid pre-event factor identified, with no development.

Credit: advantages — infrastructure (roads/rail/broadband), construction jobs, commercial investment, tourism bookings, raised national/city profile. Disadvantages — bid cost risk, construction cost overruns, displacement of residents, noise/disruption during build phase, political opposition from local community.

practice_questions.text: Identify two organisations that assess bids for major sporting events. For each organisation, name the event they award.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct organisation-event pairing (maximum 2 marks):
- IOC (International Olympic Committee) — awards the Summer and Winter Olympic Games
- FIFA — awards the FIFA World Cup
Also accept: IOC for Paralympic Games (awarded alongside the Olympics to the same host city).
Do not award for naming the organisation alone without its associated event.

lessons.title: National Governing Bodies & Technology in Sport

before.content_html:
What Are National Governing Bodies?

National Governing Bodies (NGBs) are the organisations that run individual sports within the UK. Each sport has its own NGB, and they are responsible for everything from setting the rules of the game to ensuring players are protected and the sport continues to grow. Named examples you need to know include: The FA (Football Association, governing football in England), RFU (Rugby Football Union, governing rugby union in England), ECB (England and Wales Cricket Board, governing cricket), and LTA (Lawn Tennis Association, governing tennis in Great Britain). Others include England Athletics and British Cycling.

Key Fact

The four NGBs you must be able to name are: The FA (football), RFU (rugby union), ECB (cricket) and LTA (tennis). Each governs its sport by promoting participation, developing coaching and officiating, organising competitions, amending rules, and supporting anti-doping.

Functions of an NGB

NGBs carry out several key functions. Promoting participation: NGBs run campaigns and initiatives to attract new players and retain existing ones — the FA’s “Biggest Kick” grassroots football programme is one example of community-level recruitment. Developing coaching and officiating: NGBs set standards and deliver qualifications for coaches and referees, ensuring the sport is well led at every level. The RFU, for example, manages the England Coaching Framework and referee development pathways at county level.

Organising competitions: NGBs run the competition structures from national leagues and cups down to regional and club competitions. The ECB manages domestic cricket from the Hundred through to county cricket and recreational leagues. Amending rules: NGBs can update playing regulations to improve safety, spectator experience or fairness — law changes in rugby union (restrictions on high tackles) have been driven by the RFU and its international counterpart. Anti-doping: NGBs work alongside UKAD to enforce anti-doping policies in their sport and educate athletes about clean sport.

Examiners report that students frequently write about “the NGB” in general terms without naming a specific body, and lose marks as a result. The mark scheme for “Describe with Example” or “Explain” questions on NGBs almost always requires a named NGB and a sporting example of its function in action. Practice pairing the NGB with a real initiative: The FA + grassroots football funding; RFU + coaching qualifications; ECB + the Hundred (bringing new audiences to cricket); LTA + the Great British Tennis Weekend (free courts for all).

Technology in Sport — An Overview

Technology has transformed modern sport from multiple directions: it helps athletes perform better, officials make fairer decisions, medical teams keep players safer, and spectators enjoy a richer experience. Examiners want students to analyse technology through at least two of these lenses, not just describe one device.

Key Fact

Technology in sport affects four groups: athletes (performance and safety), officials (accuracy of decisions), spectators (engagement and experience), and the sport itself (reputation and flow of the game). When evaluating technology, always consider the impact on more than one of these groups.

Technology Helping Officials

VAR (Video Assistant Referee) was introduced into the Premier League in the 2019–20 season. VAR allows a team of officials in a video operations room to review four categories of decision: goals, penalty incidents, red card offences, and cases of mistaken identity. Supporters argue that VAR eliminates clear and obvious errors that previously changed match outcomes unjustly. Critics argue that it disrupts the flow of the game, introduces inconsistency in how “clear and obvious” is interpreted, and undermines the spontaneity of goal celebrations.

Hawk-Eye operates differently in different sports. In tennis, it tracks ball trajectory to determine whether a shot landed in or out. In cricket, it is part of the Decision Review System (DRS), showing whether a delivery would have hit the stumps (LBW decisions). In football, GoalLine technology (similar in principle) determines definitively whether the ball has crossed the goal line. These systems remove human error from objective factual decisions — “did it cross the line?” — and are widely accepted as positive improvements.

GPS performance vests are worn by football and rugby players in training and in some competitions, tracking distance covered, sprint speed, heart rate and work rate zones. Coaches use this data to monitor training loads and reduce injury risk. Prosthetic limbs — particularly carbon-fibre running blades used by Paralympic sprinters — are an example of technology dramatically transforming what was previously thought possible in athletic performance. Video analysis software allows coaches and athletes to break down technique, study opponents and identify weaknesses with a precision impossible by eye alone. Wearable sensors in rugby helmets measure impact force, helping medical staff identify potential concussion incidents in real time.

Technology and the Spectator Experience

Technology also shapes how fans experience sport. Large stadium screens (known as jumbotrons) show replays, statistics and highlight close-ups, keeping spectators engaged even in the largest venues. Television broadcasting uses slow-motion cameras, ball-tracking graphics and data overlays (e.g. passing maps in football, wagon-wheel charts in cricket) to deepen understanding for viewers at home. Fan apps and in-stadium Wi-Fi allow spectators to access statistics, order food or watch replays in real time on their phones. These innovations have made watching sport more informative and immersive than at any previous time.

Despite its benefits, technology in sport creates problems. Cost and unequal access: VAR systems, Hawk-Eye installations and GPS tracking kits are expensive. Premier League clubs can afford them; grassroots clubs cannot. This creates a technological divide between elite and amateur sport that can feel unfair. Flow of the game: VAR in football has been widely criticised for long delays during which crowd atmosphere deflates and the natural momentum of the match is lost. Undermining officials: when technology frequently overturns referee decisions, confidence in human officiating can erode — both among spectators and among officials themselves. Data privacy: GPS vests and biometric trackers generate detailed personal data about athletes that raises questions about storage, ownership and consent.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the National Governing Body for cricket in England and Wales?
A) The FA
B) The LTA
C) The ECB
D) The RFU
practice_questions.marks: C) The ECB (England and Wales Cricket Board) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two functions of a National Governing Body.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct function (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
- Promoting participation in the sport
- Developing coaching standards and qualifications
- Developing officiating standards
- Organising competitions (national leagues, cups, etc.)
- Amending and enforcing the rules of the sport
- Supporting anti-doping / working with UKAD
- Providing insurance, technical guidance or safety standards
- Lobbying for funding from Sport England or UK Sport
Do not award a second mark for the same function rephrased.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which VAR (Video Assistant Referee) has improved football, and one way in which it has been criticised.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: one benefit of VAR correctly described (e.g. eliminates clear and obvious errors in goals, penalties, red cards or mistaken identity; prevents incorrect results)
- 1 mark: one criticism correctly described (e.g. disrupts the flow of the game; long delays kill atmosphere; inconsistent interpretation of 'clear and obvious'; undermines officials' authority)
- 1 mark: development or application of either point (e.g. explaining why delayed celebrations reduce spectator enjoyment; naming the four categories VAR can review; explaining how frequent overturns erode referee confidence)

practice_questions.text: Describe how technology has helped to make sport safer for participants. Use a named example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit must include at least two distinct safety-related uses of technology AND a named example:
- GPS/wearable vests monitor training load, heart rate and sprint speeds, reducing overtraining and injury risk in football and rugby
- Wearable sensors in rugby headgear measure impact force, alerting medical staff to potential concussion in real time
- Prosthetic carbon-fibre limbs allow Paralympic athletes to compete with reduced injury risk and improved mobility (named: Paralympic sprint blades)
- Video analysis / slow-motion review allows medical teams to study injury mechanisms and inform prevention programmes
- Rule changes informed by data analysis (e.g. high-tackle restrictions in rugby, informed by concussion data from RFU medical teams)
A named example is required. An answer with no named technology is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Ferndale Rovers is a semi-professional football club in West Wales. Their chairman is considering investing in GPS performance vests for the squad and a basic video analysis system.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of introducing technology into a semi-professional football club like Ferndale Rovers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion covering advantages and disadvantages, developed beyond assertion. Points interact (e.g. the data advantage must be weighed against the cost burden for a semi-professional club). The Ferndale scenario is applied meaningfully — advantages discussed in the context of a club at that level, not just elite sport. More than two distinct points on each side.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two valid points on different sides with some development. Scenario referenced but not fully applied.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid points identified, likely one-sided or very thin development.

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid point about technology in sport with no development.

Credit advantages: injury risk reduction; improved coaching decisions; better understanding of player fitness; competitive edge. Credit disadvantages: high upfront cost for a semi-professional budget; ongoing subscription/maintenance costs; requires staff training to interpret data; risk of over-reliance on data over coach judgment; data privacy concerns for players.

practice_questions.text:
'Technology has done more harm than good for sport.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Sophisticated evaluation presenting strong arguments on both sides. Arguments for (harm): VAR disrupts flow and atmosphere; cost creates inequality between elite and grassroots; frequent overturns undermine officials; data privacy risks. Arguments against (benefit): accurate decisions (Hawk-Eye, GoalLine tech); safety improvements (GPS load monitoring, concussion sensors); performance analysis unlocking athlete potential; enhanced spectator experience at broadcasts. A clear, justified conclusion is reached, not just stated — e.g. 'technology has improved accuracy and safety but has introduced unintended consequences for the spectator experience, particularly with VAR; on balance, the benefits outweigh the harms if technology is implemented thoughtfully.' Applied sporting examples used throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): Clear argument on both sides with relevant examples. Conclusion present but may not be fully justified.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some argument on both sides; evidence limited or one-sided.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Single-sided answer or simple assertions with no real evaluation.
